I am sitting at a window that overlooks a small patch of garden, and the evening is doing what evenings do best: it is turning ordinary things into silhouettes. The apple tree has become a dark scribble against a pale orange sky. The fence posts are leaning into shadow like tired monks at prayer. There is a particular quietness that comes at this hour, when the birds have stopped arguing and the streetlamps have not yet begun their yellow vigil, and I find myself thinking about writing—why we do it, what it asks of us, what it gives back. For the past few days I have been trying to put a sentence together, not for any deadline but because the sentence wanted to be written. It had been circling me like a moth around a porch light, tapping its small body against the glass of my distracted mind. Tonight I think I finally understand what it was trying to say.

The sentence was about a summer from my childhood, but not the summer you might imagine from a neat pastoral poem. It was a sticky, wrong, interminable summer. The kind where the asphalt in the cul-de-sac softened and gave beneath your sneakers, and the air smelled of cut grass and something sour, like the inside of an old refrigerator. I was nine, maybe ten. My parents had rented a house for two months by a lake that wasn't really a lake but an overgrown quarry, green with algae and ringed by cattails. There was a dock made of splintery planks that shed hot needles into your skin. I spent hours lying on that dock, face-down, staring into the murky water, watching minnows flicker in the shadows. I believed, with the unshakable confidence of a child, that if I stared long enough I would see something extraordinary—a pike the size of a rowboat, a sunken bicycle, a chest of gold coins. I never saw any of those things. What I saw was my own reflection, trembling in the water, broken and reassembled by the ripples, and the slowly changing shape of the afternoon as the sun crawled across the sky.

I have been trying to write about that dock for years, and I keep failing because I keep trying to make it mean something. I want it to symbolize the dangerous allure of introspection, or the impossibility of knowing yourself, or the gap between imagination and reality. But the dock doesn't care about symbols. The dock is just a memory, and memories are not symbolic little gifts arranged in a row; they are more like weather systems, vast and chaotic, moving through the atmosphere of your mind, bringing rain and light in unpredictable patterns. When I try to pin down that summer, it always moves. The details I remember are not the ones I would want to remember. I can recall the exact texture of a green plastic bucket, the way its handle creaked when I filled it with water. I can recall the name of the boy who lived in the next cabin—Danny—and the way he never said my name, only called me "the city kid," half mocking and half jealous. I can recall the sound of a rowboat scraping against the dock at dusk, the hollow wooden knock that seemed to ask a question. But I cannot recall the color of my room, or what I had for breakfast, or whether the sun was out on the day I found a snapping turtle at the edge of the quarry, its shell covered with algae and tiny leeches, its prehistoric head drawn in, waiting. That turtle was the most real thing in that whole summer, and I can see it now with a clarity that shames every cloudy memory I have of my own mother's face in that period. Why is that? Why is a turtle more vivid than a parent? Perhaps because the turtle was not supposed to be there, and I was not supposed to see it. I had stumbled upon a secret, and the brain hoards secrets like a miser hoards pennies.

I remember I told Danny about the turtle. We were sitting on the dock with our feet dangling in the water, and I said, "I saw a snapping turtle today, this big," and I spread my hands wide, perhaps a foot and a half. Danny squinted at me, then at the water, and said, "That's just a regular turtle." He said it with such finality that I felt my whole body slump. I wanted to insist, to defend the magnificence of my discovery, but I didn't have the words. Also, I suspected he was right. It was probably a common snapping turtle, nothing special, common enough that Danny, who had grown up around the quarry, had seen a hundred like it. The magic was not in the turtle; it was in my seeing. And that is something I have been trying to write about since: the way attention turns the ordinary into the extraordinary, the way a single glance can alchemize a common turtle into a dragon. We go through life half-blinded by our assumptions, and then, occasionally, a crack opens in the world and we see something clearly—truly clearly—and the sight is so bright it hurts. And then we spend years trying to describe that brightness, and we always fail because brightness is not a description; it is an experience.

The writing, I have realized, is not about the thing. It is about the looking. When I try to write about the turtle, I am not trying to bring the turtle back. I am trying to bring back the quality of my attention that day—the green hum of the cattails, the smell of sun-warmed wood, the flicker of a dragonfly over the water, the way time seemed to slow and thicken, like honey, so that the turtle's head emerging from its shell took a full minute, an hour, a lifetime. That quality of attention is what we lose as we grow up. Children are masters of it. They can spend an hour watching an ant carry a crumb. They can study the pattern of a leaf until it becomes a universe. They can be present in a way that adults—forsaken, distracted, always reaching for their phones—have bargained away for a handful of achievements. And writing, for me, is an attempt to get it back. When I sit at my desk and struggle to find the right word, I am not struggling to be clever; I am struggling to look more carefully. The word is just a net I throw out to catch the shimmering thing that is always slipping away.

There is a strange relationship between memory and writing. If we write a memory down, we often feel we have preserved it, but in fact we have replaced it. The story we write becomes the thing we remember, and the original experience—the raw, unmediated, messy experience—fades and shrinks until it is just a ghost of the story. I have noticed this with my own childhood. I have written about my grandparents' house so many times that I can no longer separate the house I actually visited from the house I have described. Did the kitchen really have yellow linoleum with a pattern of tiny orange flowers? Or did I invent that to add a spot of color to a paragraph? I will never know. The original house is gone, either way. It was torn down years ago, and now there is a paved driveway and a lawn of synthetic grass where the peonies used to grow. But even when I was a child, the house was never fully present to me; I was always a little too young, a little too distracted, a little too eager for it to be over so I could go home. Memory is not a recording. It is a reconstruction, and each time we reconstruct, we alter the blueprints. We are all unreliable narrators of our own lives, and that is not a flaw; it is the only way we can survive. If we remembered everything exactly as it was, we would drown in the sheer volume of details. The editing is essential. But the editing also means that we never truly possess our past. We only possess our versions of it, and those versions drift like ice floes, constantly breaking apart and colliding and re-freezing in new shapes.

I have been thinking a lot about time, too. Not the clock time, the relentless tick-tock that governs our appointments and our deadlines. I mean the other time, the time that exists inside us, the time of the mind, which is not a line but a landscape. In that landscape, the summer of the quarry is not behind me; it is just a valley I can walk to whenever I close my eyes. My grandmother is not dead; she is sitting in the same armchair, in the same patch of sun, reading the same magazine, and if I walk into that room in my mind, she will look up and smile and ask me if I want a glass of lemonade. The moments of our lives are not arranged chronologically like beads on a string; they are scattered like leaves in a forest, and we can wander among them freely. This is what Proust understood when he wrote about the madeleine—the way a small sensory trigger can dissolve the distance between past and present, so that the taste of a cookie soaked in tea becomes a portal, a time machine, a bridge over the abyss of the years. We live in a culture that worships chronological time, that measures everything, that fears age and death and change. But inside us, there is another clock, and it is not running anywhere. It is just a great still circle, a banyan tree with roots in the sky, a lake with no outlet.

I think writing is an attempt to live in that other time. When I write, I am trying to step out of the flow. I am trying to make a square of stillness, a small enclosure where the world is not moving too fast to be seen. I write to slow down. I write to pay attention. I write because I am terrified that I will forget—not the facts, but the feeling, the weight, the texture of being alive at this particular moment in this particular body in this particular century. And so I make little monuments of words, little cairns on the trail, hoping that when I come back to them later I will be able to find the path again. Sometimes it works. Sometimes I read an old essay or a journal entry and the feelings come rushing back, not as memory but as presence. I am again standing on the dock; the summer is again around me; the turtle is again emerging from the water. The words have summoned the ghost, and for a moment the ghost is more solid than I am.

But there is another side to writing, a darker side, that I must also acknowledge. Writing can become a way of not living. I can spend so much time trying to capture life that I forget to have it. The sentence I have been trying to write about the dock is a good example. I have been chasing it for weeks, and in those weeks I have not been to the lake, not walked along the shore, not felt the sun on my neck. I have been sitting at my desk, inside my own head, wrestling with syntax. And the sentence, in its stubbornness, has taught me a lesson: it will not be written because it does not want to be written. It wants to be lived. It wants me to go out into the world and find the turtle again, not in memory but in fact. It wants me to stop trying to capture the past and to start paying attention to the present. The moment I understood that, the sentence stopped circling and landed. It landed on the page, and it was not the sentence I had imagined. It was simpler. It was: You are still looking for something you found long ago, and you will not find it again because you have already found it. That is the whole point of a treasure hunt: the treasure is not at the end of the map; the treasure is the walking.

I have been thinking about my friend Elena, too, in this context. We met in college, in a workshop on creative writing, and we became friends because we both liked to sit in the back row and take notes obsessively, filling the margins with little drawings of birds. We graduated, moved to different cities, promised to keep in touch, and then did what most people do: we disappeared into our lives. Our contact dwindled to the occasional birthday text, the occasional like on a photo, the occasional "we should catch up" that neither of us truly meant. Then last spring, I was in her city for a conference, and I wrote to her, and we met for dinner at a small restaurant near the river. We talked for three hours. We talked about our jobs, our relationships, our fears, our dreams, our parents' aging, our own aging. We talked about the workshop, the professor who had told us we would never be writers, the laughter we had shared when he failed us. And at some point, Elena said something that I have not stopped thinking about since. She said, "I used to think that the point of life was to collect memories, but now I think it's to lose them." I asked her what she meant. She said, "When you are young, you think you are building a scrapbook. You think every experience is a photo you are storing for later. But then you get older, and you realize that the photos are fading, and that's okay. The point was to be there. The point was to take the photo, not to keep it. The point is the moment itself, and the moment is always leaving. All you can do is wave goodbye."

I think about Elena's words whenever I struggle with my own need to record. There is a grief in writing, a grief that comes from knowing that the words are not the experience, that the map is not the territory, that the description of the turtle is not the turtle. But maybe that grief is also a gift. It keeps us humble. It keeps us aware of the gap between language and life, and that gap is where all wonder lives. If our words could perfectly capture the world, the world would become redundant. We would not need to get out of bed; we could just read the description of getting out of bed. The fact that language always fails, always falls short, always leaves something out—that is what makes language necessary. That is what pushes us back into the world, shoves us out the door, makes us go walking in the evening with no purpose except to see the apple tree become a silhouette and to feel the cool air on our skin and to know, in our bones, that this moment will never come again and that it is enough that it came at all.

I look at the apple tree now, and I think about the first time I saw it. That was three years ago, when I moved into this house. The tree was young then, a sapling, with a trunk thin as a wrist. It was planted by the previous owner, a retired schoolteacher who loved birds and kept a feeder on the fence. I have watched the tree grow. I have watched it blossom in the spring and drop its apples in the autumn, small green things that are too sour to eat but are good for feeding the wasps. I have watched it change with the seasons, and I have written about it in my journal more times than I can count. I have tried to capture its spring finery, its summer shade, its autumn bareness, its winter black branches against the snow. And every year, I fail. The tree is always more than my words. But that failure is not a bad thing. It is a reminder that the tree is alive, that it is not a symbol, that it is not a metaphor for anything, that it is simply a tree, and that the most respectful thing I can do for it is to stop trying to own it in words and to just sit and look at it. And that is what I am doing now. I am sitting and looking. The sky has deepened from orange to magenta. A few stars have appeared, faint, tentative, like first drafts. The tree is almost invisible now, a black mass against the dusk. The window is slightly open, and I can hear the crickets beginning their chirring. The air smells of damp earth and lilac. I am not writing anymore. Or rather, I am writing the way the tree grows—slowly, without thought, without the need to be read. I am writing this essay, but I am also ending it, and the ending is not a conclusion. The ending is just a pause. It is a breath. It is the moment when the window darkens and I turn away, and the sentence that has been circling me all these weeks finally goes to rest, and I understand that it was never about the dock or the turtle or the summer. It was about this: the act of attention, the willingness to sit, the choice to be present for the quiet hour when the world reveals itself not as a story but as a presence. And that presence is the only thing worth writing about. And it is also the only thing that cannot be written. So we write anyway. We write because we are human, and humans make marks, and the marks are our way of saying to the universe, I was here, I saw this, I cared. And the universe, in its vast indifference, does not answer. But the tree answers, in its way. The crickets answer. The sky answers, turning, turning, turning to the deep blue of night. And I answer too, by sitting, by looking, by being, for a moment, the one who watches.
